entries.narration: Before learning Spark, it is worth asking whether you need it at all, because the honest answer is often no. Here is a retail chain's order events for one morning, six of them, each a line of JSON with an order ID, a store, an amount, a status and a time. The script in the editor is ordinary pandas. It loads the whole file into memory, keeps the completed orders, and adds up sales per store: sixty-five for store seven, fifteen for store nine, eighty for store twelve. For six events this is the right tool, and it finishes before you can blink. The second half of the script asks a more useful question: what does one event cost? On disk it is about a hundred and fourteen bytes. Once pandas has loaded it, with every value a Python object, it takes about a hundred and fifty-five. Now scale that up. The real chain writes about two hundred gigabytes of these events every day. At the same ratio, loading one day into pandas would need about two hundred and seventy gigabytes of memory, which is more than almost any single machine you would rent for the job. And memory is only the first wall. The table on the right uses one assumption that this whole course keeps: a machine can scan about two gigabytes a second. One day is a hundred seconds of scanning, which is fine. A year of history, around seventy terabytes, is about ten hours on one machine, and a backfill that takes ten hours cannot run every night. Spread the same year over fifty machines and each scans only one point four terabytes, all at the same time, in about twelve minutes. That is the case for distributed processing, and the list on the right is the rule for when to use it: when the data will not fit in one machine's memory, when one machine cannot finish inside the time you have, or when the data is growing faster than machines are. If none of those is true, stay on one machine. It is simpler, and it is usually faster. Next, the two ways to get more machine: a bigger one, or more of them.

When one machine is too small, there are two ways to grow. On the left is scaling up: buy a bigger machine, with more cores, more memory and faster disks. Its great virtue is that nothing about the program changes. The pandas script from the last section would simply run, because there is still only one computer and nothing to coordinate. But the trade has three costs. Near the top of the range, price climbs faster than size, so the last doubling of memory costs far more than the first. There is a largest machine you can buy, and the data does not stop growing when you reach it. And when that one machine fails, the whole run fails with it. With our year of seventy terabytes, the big machine still scans for about ten hours. On the right is scaling out: instead of one large machine, many ordinary ones. Fifty machines each hold one point four terabytes and scan it at the same moment, so the year takes about twelve minutes. Capacity grows by adding a machine rather than replacing one. But scaling out changes the program. The work has to be split into pieces that can run apart, one piece per machine at a time. Some pieces need each other's data, like every order for the same city, and that data has to cross the network, which is far slower than memory. And with fifty machines, one of them failing is not a disaster but a Tuesday, so the system must expect failure and redo only the lost piece. The table at the far right is the whole trade in five rows. Scaling up has a ceiling, a steep cost curve, and stops on a failure, but needs no coordination. Scaling out has no ceiling, grows roughly in proportion to the work, and survives failure, but every gain is paid for in coordination. Spark is a system for scaling out that makes the coordination its job, not yours. Next, the idea that makes it possible: splitting the data into partitions and sending the work to where they live.

Scaling out starts with one decision: cut the data into pieces. Spark calls a piece a partition, and when it reads files it aims for partitions of about a hundred and twenty-eight megabytes, a default you will meet again as a setting. One day of our events, two hundred gigabytes, becomes about sixteen hundred partitions. A partition is the unit of work: one task processes one partition, from start to finish, and many tasks run at once. In the middle are three machines of a cluster, each storing some of the partitions. The important choice is what moves. The naive approach would copy every partition to one place and add them up there, which sends two hundred gigabytes over the network for an answer that fits on a postcard. Instead, the code moves to the data. A function is a few kilobytes; a partition is a hundred and twenty-eight megabytes. So each machine runs the summing code on the partitions it already holds and produces a partial sum, and only those small partial results cross the network to be combined into the final answer. That is the note at the bottom right, and it is the most important rule in distributed data processing: move as little data as you can, and when you must move it, move it after you have made it small. Spark has a name for how well it manages this, locality, and the table shows its levels. Best is process local, where the data is already in the memory of the process running the task. Then node local, on the same machine's disk. Then rack local, one network hop away in the same rack. And finally any, where the data must travel across the cluster. Spark's scheduler waits a short time for a slot at a better level before it settles for a worse one. Some work cannot be done locally at all. Adding up sales per city needs every order for Leeds in the same place, wherever it started, and that movement is called a shuffle. We will spend a lot of this course on shuffles, because they are where distributed jobs spend their time. Next, where Spark came from, and the system it replaced.

Spark did not invent distributed data processing. It improved on a system that had already proved the idea. In two thousand and four, Google published the MapReduce paper: split the input, run a map function on every piece, shuffle the results by key, and run a reduce function on each group, all on cheap machines that were expected to fail. Hadoop brought an open-source MapReduce, with its distributed file system HDFS, to everyone else. Look at the top left. MapReduce runs one map and one reduce per job, and every job ends by writing its output to HDFS, replicated across machines for safety. A pipeline of several steps becomes several jobs, each reading back from disk what the last one just wrote. For a single pass that is acceptable. For an iterative algorithm that reads the same data twenty times, or an analyst asking one question after another, it is painfully slow. Spark began at the University of California, Berkeley, in two thousand and nine, precisely for those workloads. Below it, the same kind of pipeline in Spark is one plan: read, filter and join, aggregate, write. Data stays in memory between the steps and touches disk once, at the end. The list underneath says what changed. The whole pipeline is planned and optimised before anything runs. Intermediate results stay in memory instead of on HDFS. And fault tolerance comes from lineage rather than replication: Spark remembers how each partition was computed, so if a machine is lost, it recomputes just the partitions that were on it. That idea was the subject of the RDD paper in twenty twelve. On the right is the timeline in three eras. Spark became a top-level Apache project in two thousand and fourteen and reached version one that May. Spark two, in twenty sixteen, made DataFrames and the SparkSession the centre of the API and introduced Structured Streaming. Spark three added Adaptive Query Execution, which re-plans a query while it runs. And Spark four, in May twenty twenty-five, turned on ANSI SQL behaviour by default and made Spark Connect a first-class way to talk to a cluster. This course runs on Spark four point zero point one. Next, what Spark covers, and the pipeline we will build with it.

Spark is a broad system. It has SQL and DataFrames for structured data, Structured Streaming for data that keeps arriving, and libraries for machine learning and graphs. This course uses the first two, in Python, through PySpark, and leaves machine learning and graphs for courses of their own. Instead of a tour of features, we will build one application from an empty folder, and learn each part of Spark at the moment the application needs it. This is that application. On the left are its sources: a file of order events for each day, in JSON, like the six you have already seen, and a small CSV of the chain's stores, mapping store seven to Leeds, nine to York and twelve to Hull. In the middle is the batch job, one Spark application in a file called daily sales. It reads the events with a declared schema. It cleans them: parsing, validating, removing duplicates, and setting the bad rows aside rather than silently dropping them. It enriches each order with its store's city. It summarises the completed sales per city and per day. And it writes the summary as Parquet files, partitioned by day. The numbers on each step are the course where we build it. On the right is the result for the sample day, from a real run of the finished logic: Hull eighty, from one order; Leeds sixty-five, from two; York fifteen, from one. The cancelled order in York and the pending one in Leeds are correctly left out, and you will see exactly how, and what goes wrong when they are not. Below the result is the same summary as a stream, which keeps the table up to date as new events arrive, and copes with events that arrive late. Around the pipeline are the courses that are not about a new step but about the job itself: how Spark runs it, starting the project, looking underneath at RDDs, reading its query plans, making it fast, and shipping it to production. By the end you will have built every file of it, and seen every number on screen produced by Spark itself. Next, how Spark actually runs your code.

This course runs every example on one machine, in a small folder of scripts, and this is the first of them. It does the same job as the pandas script from the last course: read the six orders, keep the completed ones, and add up sales per store. The answer at the bottom of the terminal is the same too: sixty-five, fifteen and eighty. What happened on the way there is completely different, and the table on the right walks through it in order. Line seven asks for a Spark session. In PySpark that does something you might not expect: it starts a Java virtual machine. Spark is written in Scala and runs on the JVM, and your Python program is a client that drives it. That is why the very first line in the terminal is a warning from Java about a module it loaded. The JVM it started is the driver, the process that plans and coordinates all the work. Lines ten to fourteen read the file with a declared schema, filter, group and sum, and here is the surprising part: none of them reads or computes anything. Each call crosses from Python into the JVM and adds a step to a plan. Line fifteen calls show, which is an action, a request for an actual result. Only now does the driver take the plan, optimise it, cut it into stages, and hand the work to executors as tasks, one task per partition of the data. The executors run them and send the rows back, and Python prints them. Line six is the one piece of housekeeping. It points Spark at the folder named conf, which holds two small files: one keeps Spark's own log messages to warnings, so the terminal shows your output rather than Spark's chatter, and one turns off a progress bar. Every script in this course does the same. Over the next seven sections we will open up each row of that table: who the driver and executors are, how the client talks to them, why nothing ran until line fifteen, and what a stage and a task really are. Next, the cast of characters: the driver, the executors and the cluster manager.

Every Spark application has the same cast, and the diagram on the left shows it on a real cluster. Your Python process talks, through a bridge called Py4J, to the driver: one Java process per application. Inside the driver are three parts worth naming. The Spark session, with the SparkContext underneath it, is the entry point and holds the application's configuration. The DAG scheduler takes each job and cuts it into stages. And the task scheduler sends each stage's tasks to wherever there is a free slot. The driver does not own any machines. It asks a cluster manager for them, and the cluster manager, Spark's own standalone manager, YARN from the Hadoop world, or Kubernetes, starts executors on worker machines. An executor is another Java process. It has a number of task slots, one per core it was given, and memory for caching partitions. Executors run tasks and report back to the driver; they never talk to your Python program directly. That is the picture for a cluster. On the right is the same question asked on this machine. The script prints the master, local four, which means no cluster manager at all: Spark runs everything inside the one JVM it started, with four task slots. It then asks Spark's own monitoring API, the same one the web interface on port four thousand and forty is built on, for the application's executors. There is exactly one, and its name gives the game away: it is called driver. In local mode the driver is also the only executor, and its four slots are four threads in the same process. That makes local mode perfect for learning, because every concept, partitions, stages, tasks and shuffles, happens for real, just on one machine. What it cannot show you is the network between machines, and we will keep that cost in mind whenever data moves. Next, a second way to reach a driver: Spark Connect.

So far, your Python process started its own driver and talked to it through Py4J, a bridge that only works between processes on the same machine. That is classic Spark. Spark four also ships Spark Connect, where the driver runs as a server, and the client sends it requests over gRPC, an ordinary network protocol. This script runs the same query both ways. The only difference is lines nine to twelve: given the word connect, the builder calls remote with local four, which starts a Spark Connect server on this machine and connects to it; otherwise it calls master, as before. Look at the terminal. Both runs count the same four completed orders. But line fourteen prints the type of session, and they differ: the classic one comes from pyspark dot sql dot session, the Connect one from pyspark dot sql dot connect. And line nineteen tries to reach the SparkContext. The classic session prints its four task slots. The Connect session raises an error whose condition is J V M attribute not supported, because a Connect client has no JVM to reach into. The table on the right is the whole difference. With Connect, the client builds an unresolved plan and sends it to the server, which analyses and runs it. DataFrames and SQL work the same on both. Anything that needs the JVM directly, the SparkContext, RDDs, some low-level settings, is classic only. In return, the client is light, can live on a laptop or in a notebook far from the cluster, can crash without taking the driver down, and can be upgraded separately from it. This course uses classic Spark, because Course seven goes underneath DataFrames to RDDs, which Connect does not offer. Where Connect behaves differently, we will say so. Next, the reason nothing happened until show: lazy evaluation.

In the first script, four lines of Spark code did nothing until show was called. This script proves it, using the driver's own record of the jobs it has run. A new file, sample dot py, holds the six orders as Python tuples, so this and the next few scripts can build a DataFrame without reading a file. Lines twelve to fourteen make a DataFrame from them, keep the completed orders, and compute a doubled amount. Three operations, and line fifteen asks the driver how many jobs have run. The terminal says none: an empty list. Those three calls are transformations. Each returns a new DataFrame, and a DataFrame is not data. It is a plan: a description of how to compute some rows, which grows by one step with every transformation. Line seventeen calls collect, which is an action. An action asks for a result, so the driver must run the plan, and the terminal shows the four completed order IDs and one job, job zero. Line nineteen calls collect again on the same DataFrame. Another job runs, job one. Spark did not keep the rows from the first time; a second action runs the whole plan from the beginning. Course ten shows how to cache when that matters. The table on the right sorts the common calls into the two kinds. Transformations, filter, select, with column, group by and aggregate, join, order by, return a new DataFrame immediately. Actions, collect, take, show, count, writing to files, return a result or produce output, and each one runs at least one job. Why work this way? Because by the time an action arrives, Spark can see the whole plan, not one step at a time, and can optimise it as a whole: skip columns nobody uses, push a filter down into the file reader, choose how to join. You will see those optimisations in the plans of Course nine. Next, what a job is made of: partitions and the tasks that process them.

A job does its work one partition at a time, and this script counts both the partitions and the tasks that process them. The small function at lines ten to thirteen asks the driver's status tracker for the job that ran last and returns the number of tasks in each of its stages. Line sixteen makes a DataFrame of a million IDs. Spark splits it into four partitions, one for each of the four task slots, and the terminal confirms it. Line eighteen runs an action, foreach, with a function that does nothing, just so a job runs; and that job had one stage of four tasks. That is the first rule: a stage runs one task for each partition. Line twenty-one repartitions the same IDs into eight partitions, and the next action shows something new: two stages, of four tasks and then eight. Repartitioning is not free. To give every row a new partition, Spark must move rows between partitions, which is a shuffle, and a shuffle always ends one stage and starts another. The first stage reads the four original partitions and writes rows out by their new partition; the second stage's eight tasks each read one of the new partitions. The table on the right connects this to the real workload. Here, four partitions on four slots run in a single wave. Eight partitions on four slots run in two waves: four tasks, then the next four as slots free up. In production, one day of events is about sixteen hundred partitions of a hundred and twenty-eight megabytes, and fifty executors with four cores each give two hundred slots, so the reading stage runs in about eight waves. That arithmetic matters later. Too few partitions and some slots sit idle; too many tiny ones and the cost of starting each task dominates. Choosing partition sizes is the subject of a whole section in Course ten. Next, which operations can work on a partition where it is, and which must move rows: narrow and wide dependencies.

Some operations can be done on each partition by itself, and some cannot, and the difference decides where a job spends its time. Lines thirteen and fourteen filter to completed orders and select two columns. To filter a row you only need that row, so each output partition depends on exactly one input partition. Spark calls that a narrow dependency, and the top diagram on the right draws it: partition one becomes partition one, partition two becomes partition two, and nothing moves. Line seventeen groups by store and sums. To total store seven, every store-seven row must end up in the same place, wherever it started. Each output partition depends on every input partition, which is a wide dependency, and the second diagram shows the crossing lines. Line eighteen asks Spark to explain the physical plan, and the terminal shows it. Read a plan from the bottom up. Scan existing R D D reads the six rows. Filter and Project are the narrow steps from lines thirteen and fourteen; Spark even added a check that status is not null before comparing it. Then a Hash Aggregate computing a partial sum: before anything moves, each partition adds up its own rows per store, so what moves is one subtotal per store per partition, not every order. Then the line that matters most, Exchange, hash partitioning on store ID into two hundred partitions. Exchange is Spark's word for a shuffle: rows are written out, sorted by which partition they belong to, and read by the tasks of the next stage. The two hundred is the default value of spark dot sql dot shuffle dot partitions. Finally, a second Hash Aggregate adds the partial sums into final totals. Narrow operations chain together inside a stage, cheaply, partition by partition. Every wide one costs a shuffle: disk, network, and a wait for the slowest task. Next, how a job is cut into stages at exactly these points.

We now have all the words, and this script shows them fitting together on a real run. It computes completed sales per store and collects the three rows back to the driver at line eighteen. Line eleven switches off one feature, Adaptive Query Execution, for this script only. It is on by default, and it re-plans a query while it runs, which is wonderful in production and confusing in a first look; Course ten turns it back on and shows what it changes. Lines twenty to twenty-four ask the status tracker for every job, and every stage of every job, with its number of tasks. The terminal shows the hierarchy. One action, collect, made one job: job zero, which brought three rows back to the driver. The job has two stages, cut exactly where the plan had its Exchange. Stage zero has four tasks, one per partition of the input. Each task scans its partition, filters it, and computes partial sums, the narrow steps chained together, then writes its output for the shuffle. Stage one has two hundred tasks, one per shuffle partition, and each reads its share of the shuffle and finishes the sums. The diagram on the right draws the same thing. So the rule is: an action becomes a job; a job is cut into stages at every shuffle; a stage is a set of identical tasks, one per partition; and a stage cannot start until every task of the stage before it has finished, because any one of them might hold rows it needs. Look again at that two hundred. There are only three stores, so at most three of those two hundred tasks have any rows at all; the other hundred and ninety-seven start, find nothing, and finish. On six rows that costs nothing. On a real job, a badly chosen number of shuffle partitions is one of the most common reasons for slowness, and it is one of the things Adaptive Query Execution fixes. Next, what happens when one of those tasks fails.

With fifty machines, something fails on most days, and Spark's answer is not to stop. This script stages a failure so we can watch the recovery. Line eight asks for local four comma two: four task slots, and up to two attempts per task. The plain local four used so far allows only one attempt, so any failure fails the job; on a real cluster the setting spark dot task dot max failures allows four. The function on lines eleven to sixteen runs once per partition. It asks the task context which partition it is working on and which attempt this is, and on the first attempt at partition two, it raises an error, as if the executor running it had died. Otherwise it returns its partition, its attempt number and the sum of its numbers. Line nineteen spreads the numbers one to a hundred over four partitions, twenty-five each. Now the terminal. The executor logs an error for task two point zero, which means partition two, attempt zero, and the scheduler logs a warning that it lost that task; the message carries the Python traceback, which our log settings cut to its first line. And then the results: partitions zero, one and three on attempt zero, and partition two on attempt one, with a subtotal of fifteen seventy-five, exactly right. The status tracker confirms one failed task in stage zero. The table on the right shows what ran. Only partition two ran twice. The other three partitions were finished and kept; Spark did not restart the job. It could rerun that one task because the driver knows the partition's lineage: which input it came from and which functions were applied to it. Rerunning those functions on that input, on any free slot, rebuilds exactly the lost partition. That is the idea from the history section, resilience by recomputation instead of by keeping copies. It has one condition, and it will matter a great deal later: the function must give the same answer when it runs twice, and must not do anything twice that cannot be undone. Next, we start the real project.

From here on, every lesson happens in the same place: one project, shown the way your editor shows it. Before we create it, here is where it ends up, so you always know where a lesson fits. On the left is the finished folder, retail pipeline. At the top, dot venv holds the project's own Python with PySpark installed into it, and requirements dot txt records exactly which versions. The conf folder holds Spark's settings: how much it logs, and later, the defaults every run starts with. The data folder has two halves. Raw holds what the shops give us: a file of order events for every day, and the CSV of stores. Out holds what we produce: the daily sales summary, as Parquet files split into a folder per day. The jobs folder holds the two programs you will run. Daily sales is the batch job, and it is where most of this course happens. Live sales is the same summary computed continuously, as events arrive. When the rules for cleaning and checking the data grow beyond one file, they move into the pipeline package: building the session, the declared schemas, cleaning, enriching, summarising, and quality checks that every run must pass. Tools has a generator that writes millions of orders, so the query plans and timings in Courses nine and ten come from data you can make yourself. Tests holds the automated checks, and submit dot sh runs the job the way a cluster would. The table in the centre says what each part is for, and the course in which we build it. And the list on the right is how to read every lesson from now on. The tree on the left marks a file the lesson adds as new and highlights the file that is open. The centre shows that file, with this lesson's lines highlighted. Below it is the terminal, exactly as the command really ran, on PySpark four point zero point one. And when a file or an output is longer than its pane, the parts the lesson does not need are folded into a line that says how many lines it hides. Next, an empty folder, and the first command.

A PySpark project starts like any Python project, with one difference you will meet in a moment. The terminal shows every command. We make the folder and move into it. We create a virtual environment called dot venv, a private copy of Python for this project, and activate it, so that every package we install from now on goes into it rather than into the system. Then one install: pip install pyspark, pinned to four point zero point one, the version this whole course is checked against. That single package is all of Spark. Besides the Python API, it carries Spark's Java libraries and its scripts, such as spark submit, so there is nothing else to download. Pip also pulled in one dependency, Py4J, the bridge between Python and Java that you met in the last course. The next command writes the exact versions into requirements dot txt, which is the file open in the editor: py4j zero point ten point nine point nine, and pyspark four point zero point one. Anyone who installs from that file gets exactly what we ran. Now the difference. Spark runs on the Java virtual machine, so the machine needs Java, and pip cannot install that for you. The last command checks it: OpenJDK version twenty-one. Spark four supports Java seventeen and twenty-one; if java dash version says command not found, install a JDK before going further. The table on the right lists everything a PySpark project needs and what we have here: Python three point thirteen, PySpark four point zero point one, Py4J, and Java twenty-one. The last row is a cluster, and the answer is not yet. Everything until the last course runs in local mode, with Spark's driver and executors inside one process on this machine, which is enough to see every idea in this course really happen. Next, the first lines of the job itself.

The job gets its file, jobs slash daily sales dot py, and its first lines create the one object every Spark program starts from: the Spark session. The tree on the left shows two new things, the jobs folder and the conf folder. Line six points Spark at conf through an environment variable, SPARK underscore CONF underscore DIR. Spark reads two files from that folder when it starts. Log4j two dot properties keeps Spark's own messages to warnings and errors, one line each, so the terminal shows our output and not Spark's chatter; and spark defaults dot conf switches off a progress bar that would otherwise scribble over it. Setting the variable with setdefault means a real deployment can still point it somewhere else. Lines eight to ten build the session, and the table on the right takes them a call at a time. Master local four says where to run: on this machine, with four task slots. App name gives the application a name, which appears in the web interface and in the logs, and matters once many jobs share a cluster. Get or create starts the driver, or returns the one already running in this process, which is why there is only ever one session per application. Lines twelve to fourteen print what we got. The terminal shows the Java warning you met in the last course, then Spark four point zero point one, master local four, application daily sales, and the address of its web interface, on port four thousand and forty. That interface lives inside the driver and disappears when it stops, which is what line sixteen does: spark dot stop shuts the driver down cleanly. One line in this file will not survive to the end of the course. Hard-coding the master as local four is right for learning, but a real job does not decide where it runs; in Course twelve the master moves out of the code and into spark submit. Next, a faster way to try a line of PySpark before writing it into the file.

Writing a line into the job and running the whole file to see what it does costs several seconds every time, mostly to start Spark. The interactive Python prompt, the REPL, starts Spark once and lets you try as many lines as you like. Look at the command. SPARK underscore CONF underscore DIR equals conf, before the word python, sets that variable for this one command only, so the REPL gets the same quiet logs as the job. Python dash q starts the prompt without its banner. At the prompt we import the session class and build a session, and the familiar Java warning appears: getOrCreate has started the driver. Now we try a line. Create a DataFrame with one order, o1, with an amount of forty. Then type its name, df, and press enter. You might expect to see the row. Instead you see its schema: DataFrame, order ID string, amount double. That is the lesson of the last course, made visible: a DataFrame is a plan for computing rows, and printing it shows what the rows will look like, not the rows themselves. To get rows, you need an action. Collect is one, and it returns a Python list of Row objects, here a single row with order ID o1 and amount forty point zero. Notice too that Spark inferred double for the amount, a floating-point number, because we gave it forty point zero. For money that is the wrong type, and Course four declares a decimal instead. The editor still shows the job, unchanged. That is the habit worth forming: try a line in the REPL, look at what it gives you, then write it into the file. PySpark also ships its own REPL, the pyspark command, which is the same Python prompt with a session already created and named spark. Exit leaves the prompt and stops Spark with it. Next, what happens when a line in the job is wrong.

Spark programs fail in two very different ways, and telling them apart saves hours. Here is the first. The job now builds a DataFrame of three orders from lines fourteen to seventeen, with the amount as text, the way it will arrive in our files. Line eighteen selects the order ID and casts the amount to a decimal, but the column name has a typo: amout, without the n. Line nineteen prints plan built, and line twenty shows the result. Run it, and the terminal fills with more than a hundred lines. Most of them are one record: PySpark four logs every DataFrame error as a single line of JSON before raising it, which is useful to a log collector and noise to you, so the pane folds it away. What matters is at the end. The traceback starts at line eighteen of daily sales, the select. And the error is an AnalysisException with the condition UNRESOLVED COLUMN: a column, variable or function parameter named amout cannot be resolved. Spark even suggests what you meant: did you mean amount, store ID or order ID. Below that is the plan Spark was trying to build, with the unresolved column marked. The table on the right says where it stopped. The error was raised at line eighteen, when select was called. Plan built never printed. And no job ran at all. In classic PySpark, every transformation is checked by Spark's analyzer the moment it is added to the plan: are these columns real, do these types make sense, does this function exist. So a mistake in the shape of the query is caught on the driver, before a single row is read, which is cheap and fast. Learn to read these errors from the bottom: the condition in capitals names the problem, and the suggestion often names the fix. One difference to remember: Spark Connect analyses later, at the first action, so there the same typo surfaces at line twenty. Next, we fix the typo, and meet the other kind of failure.

The typo on line eighteen is fixed, so the analyzer is satisfied, and the terminal proves it: plan built is printed. The plan is valid. Then line twenty calls show, an action, and a job starts. The very next line is an error from an executor: exception in task two in stage one. Look at the data on line fifteen. Order o ten has an amount of twelve comma fifty, written the European way, and twelve comma fifty is not a number Spark can turn into a decimal. Nothing could know that until a task actually reached that row. The executor's error is followed by a line from the task scheduler: task two failed one time, aborting job. In local four there are no retries, so one failed task fails the whole job, and the error travels back to the driver and up into Python. Again the pane folds the long JSON record, and keeps the end. The error is a NumberFormatException with the condition CAST INVALID INPUT: the value twelve comma fifty of type string cannot be cast to decimal ten two because it is malformed. It suggests try cast, which tolerates bad input and returns null instead. And the last three lines are the most useful thing PySpark four adds: the DataFrame context. The cast was called from daily sales, line eighteen. The job failed at show, on line twenty, but the problem is the cast on line eighteen, and Spark points straight at it. The table on the right puts the two failures side by side. An analysis error is found by the driver, while the plan is built, before any data is read. An execution error is found by an executor, when an action runs, after reading data up to the row that breaks. Spark four's ANSI mode, which is on by default, is why this cast fails loudly rather than quietly producing a null, and that is the right default for money. Deciding what to do with malformed rows, and keeping the good ones, is the subject of Course eight. Next, real files: reading a day of order events.

Before reading real files, it is worth looking closely at the thing every read produces: a DataFrame. Lines thirteen to twenty-three build one from the six orders of our sample, written as Python tuples, with four column names. The table at the top right lists what a DataFrame has. Rows, here six of them, each one a Row object with a value for every column. Columns, with names. A schema, which is a type for every column. And partitions: the rows are spread across them, four here, one for each task slot, because every DataFrame is distributed even when it is tiny. Line twenty-four prints dtypes, the schema as a list of name and type pairs, and line twenty-five shows the first three rows. Show is an action, so it runs a job, and only three rows come back, with a note saying only the top three are shown. Now the second table, because it holds the first lesson about types. We never told Spark any types; it chose them from the Python values. Strings became string. The store number, a Python int, became bigint, a sixty-four-bit integer, which is generous for a store number but harmless. And the amount, a Python float, became double: a binary floating-point number. A double is fast, and fine for measurements, but it cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly, so ten pence plus twenty pence is not quite thirty pence, and a sum over millions of orders drifts. For money we want a decimal type with exactly two places, and the moment the data comes from a file, we will declare one. Building rows in Python, as here, is for tests and tiny examples. Real data arrives in files, and Spark reads them in parallel, partition by partition, without the rows ever passing through Python. Next, the first real file: a day of order events in JSON.

The project now has data. In the explorer, a folder data slash raw slash orders holds the first day's file, and each line of it is one JSON object: one order event, with an order ID, store, amount, status and event time. This line-per-record layout is called JSON Lines, and it is what Spark's JSON reader expects by default. Line thirteen reads it. Notice the path is the folder, not the file: Spark reads every file in a folder, which is how one job will handle many days. Line fourteen prints the schema, and the terminal shows what Spark worked out on its own. It found five columns, but look at the types. The amount is a double, because the JSON number forty point zero zero looks like a float. The event time is a string, because to JSON a timestamp is just text. The store ID is a long. And the columns are in alphabetical order, amount first, not the order they appear in the file. The table on the right compares each guess with what we actually mean. There is a cost hidden in the last line of output. Lines sixteen and seventeen ask the driver which jobs have run, and the answer is job zero, even though there is no action anywhere in this script. To infer a schema, Spark had to read the data: every line of every file, by default. On our six lines that is nothing. On two hundred gigabytes a day, it is an entire extra pass over the input before the real work begins. And the result can change from day to day: a day where every amount happens to be a whole number would be read as a long instead of a double, and code that worked yesterday would behave differently today. Inference is convenient in the REPL, when you are exploring a file you have never seen. In a job, it is a liability. Next, we tell Spark the schema instead.

Lines thirteen to sixteen declare the schema ourselves, as a string in the same syntax as a SQL table definition, and line seventeen passes it to the reader with schema, before json. The table on the right gives each choice and its reason. The order ID is a string, because it is an identifier, not something to do arithmetic on. The store ID is an int, which is plenty, and is the type the stores file will use, so the two will join cleanly. The status is a string. The event time is a timestamp: an instant, which Spark parses from the ISO text in the file. And the amount is a decimal with ten digits, two of them after the point, so forty pounds is stored as exactly four thousand pence, and sums are exact to the penny. The terminal shows the result. The schema is exactly what we declared, in the order we declared it. Then the line that matters: jobs run, an empty list. With a schema supplied, Spark had nothing to learn from the data, so it read nothing; the plan was built from our declaration alone. Line twenty-two takes the first row, which is an action, and the row it returns shows the types arriving in Python: the amount as a Python Decimal of forty point zero zero, and the event time as a datetime, nine-oh-one on the first of October, in UTC. A declared schema is a contract. It is checked against the data as it is read, it does not change when the data changes, and it costs nothing to apply. What happens when a value does not fit, an amount that is not a number, or a missing field, is the subject of Course eight. For now, every order in our file fits. Next, the second source: the stores, in CSV.

The second source is data slash raw slash stores dot csv, new in the explorer: a header line, store ID comma city, then one line per store. Seven is Leeds, nine is York, twelve is Hull. Lines eighteen to twenty-two read it with two pieces of information. The header option says the first line holds column names, not data. And the schema gives each column its type: store ID an int, city a string. The terminal shows the three stores, each in its place. Then, for contrast, line twenty-five reads the same file with neither. Look at the result: two columns, called underscore c zero and underscore c one, both strings. Without the header option, Spark treated the header line as an ordinary row, so the words store ID and city became data. And without a schema, a CSV column is always a string, because a CSV file is only text separated by commas; it has no idea that seven is a number. The table on the right lists the options that matter most. Header defaults to false. Infer schema also defaults to false; switch it on and Spark makes an extra pass to guess types, with the same costs as JSON inference. The separator is a comma by default, and is often a semicolon or a tab in files from other systems. Mode says what to do with a malformed line, and defaults to permissive, which keeps the row and puts nulls in the columns that would not parse. And null value says which text counts as missing. The lesson is the same as for JSON, only stronger. The header gives you names; only a schema gives you types. Now we can read both of the pipeline's inputs, with the types we mean. Next, how these text formats compare with Parquet, and with reading straight from a database.

JSON and CSV are text, written one row after another. Parquet, the format our pipeline will write its results in, is different, and this section shows how. Line twenty-six writes the orders out as Parquet into a scratch folder, data slash tmp, and line twenty-seven reads them back. Writing gets its own course; here we only need a Parquet copy to read. Line twenty-eight prints its types, and they are exactly the ones we declared, decimal ten two and timestamp included. Nobody supplied a schema this time: a Parquet file carries its schema inside it. Lines twenty-nine and thirty filter to completed orders, keep only the amount, and explain the plan. Read the File Scan line in the terminal. It reads only two columns, amount and status, which the read schema at the end confirms. Parquet stores each column separately, so a query that needs two columns of five reads two. And pushed filters lists the condition status equals completed: Spark hands the filter to the Parquet reader, which can skip whole blocks of rows whose stored statistics show they cannot match. JSON and CSV can do neither; to find two fields, they must read every byte of every line. The table on the right sums up what each source promises. Where the schema comes from: a scan or you for JSON, you for CSV, the file itself for Parquet, and the database for JDBC. And whether it can skip data it does not need. JDBC is the fourth kind of source: a table in a relational database, read over a database connection. There, the filter becomes part of the SQL the database runs. The list underneath, from Spark's JDBC guide, is the thing to remember: by default one task reads the whole table through one connection. To read in parallel, you name a numeric partition column, its lower and upper bounds, and a number of partitions, and Spark sends one range query per partition, all at once, each one a connection the database must be able to take. Next, we start transforming the orders: columns and expressions.

Every transformation in this course is built from one idea: an expression on columns. Line twenty-three starts a select, which builds a new DataFrame with the columns we list. The first two are plain names: the order ID and the amount. Line twenty-six is an expression: F dot col of amount, times nought point two, a value-added tax at twenty percent, named vat double with alias. F dot col does not hold any data. It names a column, and the multiplication builds a recipe that Spark will evaluate for every row, inside the engine, when an action runs. Line twenty-seven computes the same tax a second way, multiplying by a decimal literal, nought point two zero, made with Python's Decimal. And line twenty-eight adds one more column with withColumn: the gross amount, the net amount plus that tax. Look at the types in the terminal, because they are the point of this section, and the table on the right lists them. The amount is decimal ten two, as declared. Multiplied by the Python float nought point two, it became a double: one float literal, and our money silently left the exact world. Multiplied by a decimal instead, it stayed a decimal, decimal thirteen four, because Spark widens the precision so the product cannot overflow and keeps four places after the point. Adding two decimals widens it again, to fourteen four. The values agree on these tidy numbers, eight pounds of tax on forty, but over millions of rows doubles drift and decimals do not. The rule for money, then: keep every literal a decimal, and round back to two places, with F dot round, only when you present a result. Withcolumn adds a column, or replaces one of the same name. Select builds a whole new list. Both return a new DataFrame and change nothing in place, because a DataFrame is a plan, and each call extends it. Next, the built-in functions that do the real work inside those expressions.

Arithmetic only goes so far. The functions module, F, holds hundreds of built-in functions for dates, text, numbers, conditions and collections, and the pipeline needs several of them. Line twenty-four turns each event time into its calendar day with to date, which is how we will group sales by day. Line twenty-five extracts the hour. Line twenty-six lower-cases the status. And lines twenty-seven to twenty-nine are a conditional: when the status is completed, the sale is the amount; otherwise it is zero. The terminal shows the six orders through those functions. Every order fell on the first of October, all in the nine o'clock hour. The statuses are lower case. And the cancelled and pending orders have a sale of zero point zero zero, kept as a decimal because the amount was one. The table on the right lists the four functions. Two details are worth remembering. A when without an otherwise produces null for the rows that do not match, not zero, and null behaves very differently in sums and comparisons, as Course eight shows. And the day and hour depend on a time zone. An event time is an instant; which calendar day it falls on depends on where you are standing. Spark uses the session time zone, which here is UTC, so nine-oh-one UTC is the ninth hour of the first of October. In New York it would be the fifth hour. The reason to prefer these functions to your own Python code is in the list on the right: built-in functions run inside the JVM, as part of the plan, where Spark can optimise them and generate fast code. A Python function applied to each row has to ship every row out to a Python process and back. Course eight measures that difference. Next, keeping only the rows and columns we need.

The summary only counts completed orders, so the first real step of the pipeline is a filter. Line twenty-two keeps the rows where the status equals completed. Line twenty-three writes the same condition a second way: where, which is the same method by another name, given the condition as SQL text. Spark parses the text into the same expression, so the two produce identical plans. Lines twenty-four and twenty-five count both, and the terminal agrees: four of six orders completed, and four by the SQL text. Line twenty-seven then keeps only three columns, the order ID, the store and the amount, and line twenty-eight shows the four completed orders: o1 and o2 from store seven, o4 from store nine, o5 from store twelve. The cancelled order o3 and the pending order o6 are gone. The table on the right shows the three ways to write a filter, and the choice between them is style; inside Spark they are the same. What matters more is in the list. Filter keeps rows and select keeps columns, and both are narrow: each partition is filtered where it lies, and nothing moves between machines. That makes them the cheapest operations there are, and it gives the most important habit in Spark: keep less, early. Every row filtered out and every column dropped before a shuffle is data that never has to be written to disk, sent across the network, and read back. Spark's optimizer will often move a filter earlier for you, and drop columns nobody uses, but only when it can see that it is safe. Notice too that each count is an action, so this script ran its plan several times, once for every count. Next, grouping the completed orders by store, which is the first operation that does have to move data.

Line twenty-three groups the completed orders by store, and lines twenty-five to twenty-nine compute three aggregates for each group: the sum of the amounts as sales, the number of orders with count, and the average amount with avg. Line thirty orders the result by store. The terminal shows the answer: store seven, sixty-five pounds from two orders, an average of thirty-two fifty; store nine, fifteen from one; store twelve, eighty from one. Line thirty-three prints the types of the three new columns, and they repay a look. The sum is decimal twenty two: Spark adds ten digits of precision to a decimal sum, so that adding up even billions of amounts cannot overflow. The count is a bigint. The average is decimal fourteen six, which is why it prints with six decimal places, thirty-two point five zero zero zero zero zero. Round it for display, not before. Two things in the list on the right are about how this runs. Group by on its own does not return a DataFrame. It returns a grouped data object, which only becomes a DataFrame when you tell it what to compute with agg. And grouping is the first wide operation of the pipeline. Every order for store seven must end up in the same partition, wherever it was read, so Spark computes partial sums in each partition, shuffles them by store, and adds them up: the plan you met in Course two, with its Exchange in the middle. Ordering is wide as well. To sort the whole result, Spark samples the data, cuts it into ranges, and shuffles each row to the partition for its range. On three rows none of this costs anything. On a year of data, the number of shuffles in a job is the first thing to look at. Next, the city: joining the orders to the stores.

Sales per store number are not much use to the people reading the report. They want cities. Line twenty-three joins the completed orders to the stores on the store ID, with an inner join. Because we passed the column name with on, the result has a single store ID column rather than one from each side, and every order now carries its store's city. Lines twenty-four to twenty-eight then group by two things: the day, with to date, and the city, and compute the sales and the number of orders. The terminal shows the result, and it is the table from the very first course, now produced by our own job: Hull, eighty pounds from one order; Leeds, sixty-five from two; York, fifteen from one. All on the first of October. The table on the right lists the join types, because the choice is a decision about the business, not about code. An inner join keeps only orders that have a matching store. A left join keeps every order, with a null city when no store matches. A left anti join keeps exactly the orders that have no store, and a left semi join the orders that do, without adding any columns from the stores. A full join keeps everything from both sides. Lines thirty-one and thirty-two use left anti as a check: how many completed orders would the inner join silently drop? Today, none. But the inner join is a quiet filter, and an order for a store that is missing from the stores file would simply vanish from the revenue, with no error. Course eight meets exactly that, an order from store fifteen, along with the opposite danger, a store listed twice, which would double every sale it touches. Like grouping, a join is wide in general. Here Spark will be cleverer, because the stores table is tiny, as Course nine shows. Next, the same summary written as SQL.

Everything we built with DataFrame calls can also be written in SQL, and many teams prefer it. Lines twenty-two and twenty-three register the two DataFrames as temporary views, called orders and stores. A view is just a name: it stores no data, and refers to the DataFrame's plan, so a query against it reads the same files. Line twenty-four runs a SQL query through spark dot sql. It selects the day from the event time and the city, sums the amount and counts the orders, from orders joined to stores, where the status is completed, grouped by the first two columns, and ordered by day and city. The terminal shows the result, identical to the last section's, row for row. The table on the right maps one form to the other. A filter is a WHERE. A join is a JOIN with its ON condition. Group by and agg are GROUP BY with aggregate functions. Order by is ORDER BY, and alias is AS. These are not two engines. Spark parses the SQL into the same kind of plan the DataFrame calls build, and from there both go through the same analyzer and optimizer to the same physical plan, so neither is faster. Spark dot sql returns an ordinary DataFrame, so you can mix the two freely: a SQL query, then a DataFrame filter on its result, then a write. Choose by readability: SQL for a query a data analyst will maintain, DataFrame calls when the logic is assembled by Python code, such as columns chosen in a loop. The last line lists the session's catalog, and shows both views with the type temporary. A temporary view belongs to this Spark session and disappears when it stops. Next, something that does not disappear: a table.

A temporary view is a name for a plan. A table is a name for data. Line twenty-nine writes the daily summary with save as table, under the name daily sales, and line thirty registers the orders as a temporary view again, so we can compare the two. Lines thirty-two and thirty-three walk the catalog, and the terminal shows both: daily sales is a managed table, and orders is temporary. Line thirty-four reads the table back by its name, with spark dot table, and shows the three rows. The second command in the terminal looks at the disk. Save as table wrote real files, into a folder called spark warehouse, which has appeared in the explorer: a Parquet file, whose long name ends in a random identifier, and an empty file called underscore success, which Spark writes last to say the write finished. Managed means Spark owns both the name and the files: drop the table, and its folder goes too. The table on the right sets the two side by side. A temporary view stores nothing and lives for one session. A managed table stores Parquet files under the warehouse folder, and its files stay when the session ends. There is a subtlety in the last row of the list. Where the name is kept depends on the catalog, and the one this session uses is Spark's built-in in-memory catalog: it forgets the name when the session stops, even though the files remain. On a real platform the catalog is a shared metastore, such as a Hive metastore or a cloud data catalog, so every job and every analyst sees the same table names, and Course twelve comes back to it. For our pipeline we will not rely on names at all. The summary will be written to a path we choose, in data slash out, which is what the next course does. Next, writing the results.

Until now the job has printed its results. A pipeline has to store them, and line twenty-eight does: write, with mode overwrite, as Parquet, to data slash out slash daily sales. Lines thirty and thirty-one read it straight back to prove it, and the terminal shows three rows, with every column's type intact: the day is a date, the sales are decimal twenty two, the count a bigint. Nobody declared those types on the way back in, because Parquet stores the schema with the data. The second command lists what Spark actually wrote, and it is not a file. Daily sales is a folder. Inside it are two things. A part file, part zero zero zero zero zero, with a long random identifier and the suffix snappy dot parquet, meaning its columns are compressed with Snappy. Spark writes one part file for each partition of the DataFrame it writes, each written by its own task, in parallel, which is why output is always a folder; here the summary had one partition, so there is one file. The random identifier keeps two writers from ever choosing the same name. And underscore success, an empty file Spark writes last, once every task has finished, so anything reading the folder can tell a complete result from one still being written. The table on the right lists the four save modes, and the default deserves care. Error if exists is the default: write to a path that already exists, and the job fails. That protects you from overwriting something by accident, but it also means a job that ran yesterday fails today. Overwrite deletes everything in the path and writes afresh, which is what a daily job that recomputes its summary wants. Append adds new files beside the old ones, so running twice doubles the data. Ignore silently does nothing if the path exists. Choosing the mode is choosing what a rerun means. Next, splitting the output into a folder per day.

A second day of orders has arrived, the second of October, and the explorer shows its file beside the first. Four more orders, one of them cancelled. The job reads the whole orders folder, so it now summarises both days without any change. Lines twenty-eight to thirty-two change the write: partition by day. The second command in the terminal finds every Parquet file Spark wrote, and the layout has changed. Inside daily sales there is now a folder per day, named day equals twenty twenty-six dash ten dash zero one, and day equals twenty twenty-six dash ten dash zero two, each with its own part file. The day column is no longer stored inside the files at all; it is in the folder names. Lines thirty-three to thirty-five read the whole output back, keep only the second of October, and show it: Hull forty-five, Leeds thirty, York twenty. Notice that the day comes back as the last column. Spark rebuilds it from the folder names, and puts partition columns at the end. That filter is where partitioning pays. Because the day is in the path, Spark can see from the folder names alone which folders hold the second of October, and never opens the others. That is called partition pruning, and the table on the right shows it: asking for one day reads one folder; not filtering on day reads them all; filtering on the city cannot prune, because the city is inside the files. With a year of history, a query for one day reads one three hundred and sixty-fifth of the data. Choose the partition column by how the data is read: something readers filter on, with a modest number of values, like the day. Partitioning by order ID would make one folder per order, millions of tiny files, and the cost of listing and opening them would swamp any saving. Next, bringing results back to the driver, and how much is too much.

Sometimes a result has to leave Spark and come into your Python program: to print it, to put it in an email, or to make a decision. Every action that returns data brings it to the driver, and the driver is a single process on a single machine. Line twenty-nine calls collect, which brings every row of the summary into this Python process as a list of Row objects. The terminal shows six rows, and the first one: the first of October, Hull, eighty pounds, one order, with the day as a Python date and the sales as a Decimal. Six rows is nothing. But collect does not know or care how many rows there are, and on a DataFrame of a billion orders it would try to pull all of them through one machine's memory. Line thirty-one uses take, which asks for only as many rows as it needs, here the two smallest sales, both York. And line thirty-three counts the Leeds days, which brings back one number, two, however much data the count went through. The table on the right sorts these actions by what they bring back. Collect and to pandas bring every row; to pandas also needs pandas installed, and builds a pandas DataFrame on the driver. Take brings a fixed number. Count brings one number. To local iterator brings one partition at a time, so the driver holds only a partition's worth at once. Spark has a guard rail, in the list underneath: a setting called spark dot driver dot max result size, one gigabyte by default, and a job whose results exceed it is stopped rather than allowed to take the driver down. The habit that avoids all of this is simple. Do the heavy work on the cluster, aggregate down to something small, and only then collect. And for a large result, write it, because a write goes from the executors straight to storage and never passes through the driver. Next, the opposite direction: code that runs inside tasks, and does something to the outside world.

Our pipeline will send each completed order's receipt to the customer, and this new script, notify dot py, is a first attempt. It uses foreach partition, which runs a Python function inside every task with that task's rows, so the sending happens on the executors, in parallel, and never on the driver. The send function, from line twelve, opens a log file that stands in for an email service and writes one receipt line per order. To show what happens on a real cluster, line nine asks for two attempts per task, and lines seventeen and eighteen make the first attempt of partition zero fail after it has sent its receipts, as if its executor had died at the worst possible moment. Line twenty-four spreads the completed orders over three partitions and runs it. The terminal shows the executor's error and the scheduler's warning that it lost task zero. Spark did what it promised in Course two: it ran the lost task again, the second attempt succeeded, and the job finished. Now the last command, which sorts the receipts that were sent. Eight lines for seven completed orders. Receipt o eleven, thirty pounds, appears twice. The first attempt sent it before it died, and the retry sent it again. Spark recomputed the partition perfectly, but it cannot unsend an email. That is the rule in the list on the right. Spark retries tasks, not their effects on the outside world, and it can also run a task twice without any failure at all, when speculative execution starts a backup copy of a slow task. Anything a task does outside Spark must therefore be safe to do twice. The table lists the usual ways. Give each effect an idempotent key, so the receiving system ignores a repeat of receipt o eleven. Write with an upsert, so the second write replaces the first. Do the effect once, on the driver, after the job has finished, when the result is small. Or use a sink with transactions, which only commits when the task succeeds. Course eleven applies the same thinking to streams. Next, the whole batch job, end to end.

This is the batch job as Part one of the course leaves it, and every line of it is something we have built. The terminal runs it and reads the result back. Six rows: Hull, Leeds and York for the first of October, with the eighty, sixty-five and fifteen you have seen since the first course, and the same three cities for the second of October, with forty-five, thirty and twenty. The last command counts the Parquet files written: two, one in each day's folder. The table on the right walks through the job, and the third column is the one to keep in mind for the rest of the course: does the step move data between machines? Lines nineteen and twenty read the orders with their declared schema, and the stores with theirs. Line twenty-two keeps the completed orders, which is narrow. Line twenty-three joins each order to its store's city. A join is wide in general, but the stores table is tiny, and Spark will broadcast it, sending a copy of it to every task instead of shuffling the orders; Course nine shows that in the plan. Lines twenty-four to twenty-six sum the sales per day and city, which needs a shuffle, the one real data movement in the job. And lines twenty-eight to thirty-one write the result, a folder per day, each task writing its own files directly. Reading and writing in parallel, one shuffle, and a broadcast. That is a well-shaped Spark job. It is not yet a trustworthy one. It assumes every event is well formed, every store exists exactly once, every amount is a number, and every order arrives once; real event streams break all four. And it rewrites every day's folder on every run, which will not do once there is a year of history. Course seven first looks underneath DataFrames, at the RDDs they are built on. Then Course eight makes this job correct on messy data.

Every DataFrame in this course has been running on something older and simpler underneath: the resilient distributed dataset, or RDD. An RDD is a distributed collection of plain objects, with no schema, and its operations are ordinary Python functions. This new folder, explore, holds three short scripts that look at it, and this first one computes the completed sales per store, one level down. Line twelve reads the order files with text file, which gives an RDD of strings, one per line. Line thirteen maps each line through the JSON parser, asking for decimals for the amounts, so each element becomes a Python dictionary. Line fourteen filters with a lambda. Line fifteen maps each order to a pair, the store and the amount. And line sixteen reduces by key: for each store, add the amounts. The terminal shows the result, as Python tuples: store seven, ninety-five pounds, store nine thirty-five, store twelve a hundred and twenty-five, both days together. Line nineteen prints the RDD's lineage with to debug string, and this is the idea that made Spark. Read it from the bottom up. A Hadoop RDD reading data slash raw slash orders, then the text lines, then a Python RDD where our map and filter ran, then a pairwise RDD for reduce by key; then the marker plus dash three, which is a shuffle, the boundary between two stages; above it, folded away in the pane, are the shuffled RDD and the result. The three in brackets is the number of partitions. That chain is all Spark keeps. It does not keep the data of each step; it keeps the recipe, so that any lost partition can be rebuilt by replaying its part of the chain. The table on the right gives each line of code its RDD. The list says what you give up at this level. There is no schema, so Spark cannot know that only two fields are needed. There is no optimizer, so Spark runs exactly the steps you wrote, in that order. And every lambda runs in a Python worker process, one record at a time, with each record shipped out of the JVM and back. Next, the pair RDD operation that every Spark interview asks about.

An RDD of pairs, a key and a value, gets a family of operations by key, and two of them do the same arithmetic at very different cost. Line twelve makes a hundred thousand pairs over four partitions: the key is the number modulo three, so there are three keys, and the value is the number itself. Line fourteen sums the values per key with reduce by key. Line fifteen gets the same sums another way: group by key collects every value for a key, and then map values sums each group. The terminal shows the three sums, around one point six six billion each, and true: both ways agree. To see the difference, lines eighteen to twenty-two ask Spark's monitoring API about every stage that wrote to a shuffle. Stage zero, the reduce by key, wrote twelve records and eight hundred and sixty-eight bytes. Stage two, the group by key, also wrote twelve records, but three hundred and thirty-five thousand bytes, almost four hundred times as much. The table on the right sets them side by side. Reduce by key combines on the map side: each task adds up its own partition's values for each key before anything moves, so what crosses the shuffle is one running total per key per partition, three keys times four partitions, twelve small numbers. Group by key cannot combine, because its job is to deliver every value. PySpark packs each partition's values for a key into a list before shuffling, which is why the record count is also twelve, but each of those records carries a list of around eight thousand numbers. On a real cluster that is the difference between a shuffle you do not notice and one that fills the network. The rule generalises far beyond RDDs: reduce before you move. DataFrame aggregations do it for you, which is what the partial sum in Course two's plan was. Next, a subtler trap: what a function takes with it when it is sent to an executor.

When you pass a function to an RDD or to foreach, Spark serialises it, together with every variable it refers to, and sends that bundle, called a closure, to the executors. That has a consequence that surprises almost everyone once. Line fourteen sets a plain Python variable, counter, to zero, and the function count on lines seventeen to nineteen adds one to it for every order. Line twenty-two runs it with foreach over the completed orders, and line twenty-three prints the counter on the driver. The terminal says zero. Each task received its own copy of counter, inside its own Python worker, and added to that copy; the driver's variable was never touched. In local mode it might even appear to work sometimes, which is worse. The correct tool is on line twenty-five: an accumulator, a variable that tasks can only add to and that Spark sends back to the driver. Line twenty-six adds one per order, and line twenty-seven reads it on the driver: seven, the completed orders across both days. Lines twenty-nine and thirty show the other direction. A broadcast variable sends a read-only value, here a small dictionary from store number to city, to every executor once, and tasks read it with dot value. The result is each order named by its city, from Hull, o twelve, to York, o four. The table on the right sorts the three mechanisms by direction. A closure copies values from the driver into every task, which is fine for small values. A broadcast sends a value once per executor rather than once per task, which matters for a lookup table of real size, and it is exactly what a DataFrame broadcast join does for you. An accumulator carries numbers from tasks back to the driver, for counts and metrics. One caution in the list: an accumulator updated inside a transformation, rather than an action, can count twice if a task is retried, so use them for monitoring, not for results. Next, how to choose between all these ways of writing the same thing.

We have now written the same summary three ways, and the top row shows them side by side, each taken from a file that really ran. On the left, the RDD version from the last three sections: text in, Python dictionaries, a filter, a map to pairs, and reduce by key. In the middle, the DataFrame version from our job: a filter on a column, a join, a group by and an aggregate. On the right, the SQL version from Course five. All three produce the same numbers. They are not equal choices, and the table underneath says why. With an RDD, the rows are whatever Python objects you make, and Spark cannot see inside them, so it cannot optimise: it runs your functions in the order you wrote them, in Python worker processes, one record at a time. A mistake in a field name is found only when a task runs into it. A DataFrame and SQL have a schema, so Spark knows the columns and their types, checks your query while the plan is built, runs the work inside the JVM, and optimises the whole plan before running it: dropping unused columns, pushing filters into the reader, choosing the join. DataFrames and SQL compile to the same plans, so between those two the choice is about who maintains the code. The last column is a fourth option you will meet in Spark documentation: the typed Dataset. It is a DataFrame whose rows are objects of a class you define, so a wrong field name is a compile error, found before the program runs. That needs a compiled language with static types, Scala or Java, so Python does not have it; in PySpark a DataFrame is the whole story. The list on the right is the practical rule. Use DataFrames or SQL by default. Reach for RDDs only for data with no useful schema, or when you need direct control over partitions. And remember from Course two that RDDs are not available through Spark Connect at all. Next, Part two of the course: making the pipeline correct when the data is not.
